newsitem.title: USA: Fans flood Memphis on 20th anniversary of Elvis Presley's death.
newsitem.headline: Fans flood Memphis on 20th anniversary of Elvis Presley's death.

text.p: Elvis Presley fans flooded Memphis on Friday by the tens of thousands to mourn the 20th anniversary of his death, celebrate the rock n' roll memories he gave the world and pay silent tribute at his grave.

Some began standing in line 24 hours in advance of a candlelight vigil that was to last until daybreak on Saturday, eager to be among the first to pass through the gates of the entertainer's home for the solemn, single-file walk past his grave.

It was 20 years ago on Saturday that an ambulance crew answered an emergency call at 3764 Elvis Presley Blouevard. Inside the house, a stone-sided, white-columned southern mansion better known as Graceland, they found the street's namesake dead in his bedroom.
He was 42, and investigators would conclude he died of a drug-induced heart attack.

An estimated 50,000 people -- the biggest such crowd to gather in Memphis since Presley's funeral two decades ago -- have come to this steamy city by the muddy Mississippi River to relive old love songs, remember teen-aged crushes and tell their children how Elvis put their legs to dancing.

Thousands planned to join Friday night's vigil outside Graceland, facing the hillside where Presley, his parents and paternal grandmother are buried in a garden half-circled by trellised Corinthian columns on one side and a kidney-shaped swimming pool on the other.
Bill Rowe, a 47-year-old paper mill foreman from Dayton, Ohio, was the first in line, staking out a position 24 hours in advance. It was the 10th year in a row he has been there first.

"For me it's to pay back what I feel is a debt to an old friend," he said. "When I was growing up he taught me a few of life's lessons ... two I learned were that to make it big you don't have to trample over people and that you never get too big to remember your friends and family."

Rowe said he was part of a group of fans from across the United States who make a pact to return to Graceland and take part in the vigil yearly. They wore red shirts emblazoned "The Gates of Graceland Entourage."

During the vigil, candle-carrying fans are allowed to walk up the driveway into Graceland all nght long, circling the grave and walkng back down the hill. In advance of the ceremony Graceland remained open for regular tours and the complex was mobbed with gift-buying visitors from around the world.

Many of them took the $18.50-a-head "platinum tour" which includes not only the home and grave but several other attractions in the complex, including two customized jet planes in which Presley once toured.
Elvis Presley Enterprises, which operates Graceland and merchandises the entertainer's estate, estimates that 9 million people have visited the home since Elvis died.

Those who couldn't journey to Memphis to mark the day have sent floral designs -- artificial and real -- trinkets, stuffed animals and posters. They are strewn across the graves and stand sentry up and down the walkways leading from the Meditation Garden, as the graveyard is called. Every few minutes a guard plants one or two more late-arriving tributes.

Dolores, Linda and Polly, hometown not listed, have sent an evergreen wreath inset with a plastic miniature model of Graceland decorated for Christmas with a pink Cadillac parked outside like the one Elvis once owned.
Beth and Kathie from St. Louis, Missouri, chose a guitar, spray-painted black with a message written in gold, "20 years, 20 million tears."

"The Official Fan Club of Denmark" has sent along a bank of red carnations imbedded with a cross of white ones. On the swimming pool fence is a towel-sized banner reading "Elvis - We thank you for the freedom you gave us -- Brazilian fans." From Berlin, Edelgard and Michael have dispatched a yellow and red heart with a color photo of Elvis in the center.

At the head of his gravestone is a knee-high bronzed obelisk imprinted "Paris Remembers Elvis," a tiny tricolor fixed to its tip. Fans from Austria, New Zealand, Belgium, Britain and a number of other nations are represented as well.

The mood away from the gravesite is celebratory. Fans jam souvenir counters and restaurants, and music fills the air from a tent near the staging area where fans sometimes wait hours to take the mansion tour.

The Memphis Convention and Visitors Bureau estimated the death anniversary and events leading up to it would pour $25 million into the local economy. There are dozens of daily concerts, shows by Elvis imitators, boat rides and scholarly discussions spread across the city -- all about the young man from Mississippi who turned pop music upside down in the 1950s with a blend of blues, gospel, country and black music that became rock and roll.
